identity.title: Suprapubic palpation / percussion for distended bladder; LUTS and prostate history

technique.how: Supine: inspect for suprapubic fullness, percuss from umbilicus toward pubis for a change from tympany to dullness, and palpate for a smooth, tense midline mass that provokes urge to void. Ask about hesitancy, weak stream, incomplete emptying, prior retention, prostate disease, and new anticholinergic/opioid drugs; check perineal sensation and anal tone if a neurologic cause is possible.
technique.prerequisites: Bladder scanner or catheterization for confirmation of volume.

interpretation.positive_finding: Suprapubic dullness and a palpable tense bladder suggest retention with a large volume, especially with LUTS, prostate history, new anticholinergic/opioid, or post-operative state.
interpretation.negative_finding: A non-palpable, non-dull suprapubic area argues against a very large retained volume but does not exclude clinically important retention (several hundred mL), particularly in obese patients.
interpretation.pitfalls: Bladder is generally palpable only above ~300-500 mL and obesity, ascites, pregnancy or pelvic masses obscure or mimic it; positive predictive value of clinical assessment is low, so verify with a bladder scan before catheterizing on exam alone.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive: bladder scan/catheterize, review drugs, and consider neurologic cause; negative does not remove retention from the AKI or delirium differential, so still scan.

sources.citation: Pedersen LM, Mantoni T, Lynggaard MD, Schousboe BM, Lauritzen JB, Pedersen BD, Jorgensen HL. [Postoperative urinary retention. Clinical assessment versus ultrasound examination]. Ugeskr Laeger. 2007.
Selius BA, Subedi R. Urinary retention in adults: diagnosis and initial management. Am Fam Physician. 2008.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on percussion/palpation alone to decide against catheterization in AKI, delirium, or suspected cauda equina; a bladder scan is required.
safety_scope.escalation_warning: Retention with new saddle anesthesia, leg weakness, or back pain is a cauda equina emergency requiring urgent MRI and surgical referral.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Pedersen 2007 used two trained doctors examining 25 patients each; no agreement statistic is given in the abstract.

extraction_notes: No study reporting sensitivity/specificity or LRs for suprapubic palpation/percussion against a scanner or catheter volume was found (searches: bladder palpation percussion urinary retention; physical examination bladder volume ultrasound scanner). The only clinical-assessment-versus-ultrasound study found, Pedersen 2007 (PMID 17311756; 50 post-operative recovery-room patients, BladderScan BVI 3000 reference), reports predictive values only: 'We found a high negative predictive value of 92% for a cut-off limit of 500 ml. The corresponding positive predictive value was a modest 38%' (Abstract, Results); predictive values cannot be entered as sens/spec/LR and prevalence is not given, so estimates are empty. The frequently cited '~300-500 mL palpable' threshold is textbook teaching (unverified recall). Selius & Subedi 2008 (AFP review) cited as the consensus source for the maneuver and history items; it is a narrative review, not a guideline body statement. Bladder-scanner accuracy studies retrieved (PMIDs 29952185, 24767639, 17115233, 16411009) evaluate the device, not the exam, and were not used.
